extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, newsroom managers, and journalists interested in news selection and the sociology of news
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and organizational routines that determine which events become news and how they are covered, based on Tuchman's 1973 typification and routinization framework. Useful for analyzing newsroom decision-making and news production practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard News
rubrics_metrics.description: Information people should have to be informed citizens. Time-bound, scheduled events of public consequence (legislation, accidents, crime, fires). Drives the front-page agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard news items are prioritized for immediate and prominent coverage; they are usually time-sensitive and fit established news frames that qualify them for above-the-fold placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft News
rubrics_metrics.description: Human interest, features, lifestyle. Not time-bound; can be held and run when space is available. Lower deadline pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soft news can be scheduled flexibly and is often used to fill space; its newsworthiness is judged by audience interest and available staff/space rather than immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spot News
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden, unexpected hard news (a fire, a disaster). Requires immediate dispatch of resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot news triggers rapid reallocation of personnel and resources; newsrooms rely on pre-existing routines (e.g., who is on duty, templates) to cover it quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing News
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news whose facts are still emerging during the news cycle (an unfolding hostage crisis). Requires updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developing stories demand continuing attention and multiple updates; they often occupy resources over time and may graduate to continuing news if ongoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing News
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-known sequences of stories on a single topic stretching over days/weeks (a trial, a legislative session). Pre-scheduled and resource-allocated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a topic is classified as continuing news it enjoys a momentum or quasi-automatic newsworthiness boost; organizations allocate fixed budgets and personnel for ongoing coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling and Beat System
rubrics_metrics.description: Events anchored to known calendars (court dockets, agency briefings, sports schedules) are easier to cover and therefore more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms privilege events that fit beats and calendars because they allow planning; presence on a beat increases the likelihood of coverage due to predictable timing and reporter availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic Centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Resources concentrated near beats; events occurring outside reporter geography are systematically under-reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage skews toward events within reporters' geographic remit; lack of local beats or bureaus makes events less visible and less likely to be treated as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-allocation of Space and Personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: "Continuing news" gets fixed budgets, enabling more depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When space and staff are pre-allocated, stories receive sustained attention and deeper treatment; newsrooms make editorial commitments that shape what can be followed over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routinizing the Unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: "Spot news" is itself routinized through rotating assignments and pre-built templates (the disaster story, the obituary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations manage surprises by slotting them into pre-existing procedures and story forms, which speeds production but also shapes the narrative and limits novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedulability as an Implicit News Value
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that fit organizational scheduling are vastly more reportable than those that don't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsworthiness partly by whether an event can be slotted into existing schedules or beats; unschedulable events face higher barriers to coverage regardless of objective significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of Typification
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that fit cleanly into one of the five categories receive faster, fuller treatment; ambiguous events get less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The easier it is for newsroom staff to classify an event (hard/soft/spot/developing/continuing), the more likely it is to be covered promptly and thoroughly; ambiguity increases delay or neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing-news Momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a topic is classified as "continuing news," subsequent installments enjoy a quasi-automatic newsworthiness boost (echoes Galtung & Ruge's continuity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior classification creates inertia: editors are more likely to run follow-ups, which can perpetuate the prominence of a topic beyond its standalone news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat Capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters' assignments shape what becomes news — events outside any beat are invisible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage reflects who is on which beat; topics and locales with no assigned reporter are less likely to surface, producing systematic blind spots in news agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-page Eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hard" + "spot" or "developing" status is largely required for above-the-fold play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combination of category and immediacy determines placement: front-page prominence typically requires both substantive public importance (hard news) and timeliness or unfolding character (spot/developing).
